newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: FEATURE - Time bomb of young threatens Saudi future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Time bomb of young threatens Saudi future.

text.p: Rising numbers of unemployed youths pose a threat to the stability of Saudi Arabia, diplomats and analysts say.
"The survival of the kingdom depends on whether they will be able to get a handle on this problem or not," says one diplomat.

Long gone are the days when the world's richest oil state found work for its young in the bloated bureaucracy. While there are no official unemployment figures in Saudi Arabia, analysts say the jobless rate is above 10 percent and rising.
And with the population ballooning by an estimated 3.5 to four percent a year and half the population under 15, they say the number of frustrated youths is growing at a worrying pace.

"Huge sections of Saudi society consist of disgruntled youths," a senior Western diplomat told Reuters. "They are like the crest of a wave. It hasn't reached crisis proportions yet, but when the wave peaks it'll all come crashing down."
Diplomats say unemployed young Saudis lacking social outlets are more susceptible to influence by radical movements opposed to the royal family.
"Young people see faults in Saudi society but don't find any fault with themselves. They see the problem only with the government and the country's leadership," the senior Western diplomat said.
GOVERNMENT AWARE OF DANGER

King Fahd and his government seem fully aware of the danger and have launched a large-scale "Saudisation" drive to create more jobs for citizens and replace some of the expatriate workforce with Saudis.
The foreigners -- mostly from the Indian subcontinent, southeast Asia, Egypt and other Arab countries -- comprise about one third of the kingdom's population of 18 million.
The king emphasises the need to find jobs for youths at almost every weekly cabinet meeting he chairs. Chambers of commerce have also been pushing training programmes for Saudis.
For decades Saudi citizens enjoyed their country's oil wealth and preferred well-paid, half-day jobs in the state sector. Menial jobs and manual labour were traditionally done by expatriates.
But a squeeze on state spending, a decade of weak oil prices until last year and an estimated $50 billion spent on the Gulf War have changed the job market.
The country's 1995-2000 development plan set a target of creating 659,000 jobs for Saudis by the turn of the century, in part by phasing foreigners out of some jobs.
But analysts say the steps are not enough, as the plan foresees the size of the working-age population rising by 1.6 million in the same period.
Less than seven percent of private sector workers are Saudi, and unemployment among young people is rampant.
NOT ALL SAUDIS HAVE LAVISH LIFESTYLES
Contrary to a popular belief outside the country, not all Saudis have lavish lifestyles fueled by petrodollars. Diplomats estimate average per capita annual income at $7,000 to $8,000.

In the streets of the capital, Saudis from the countryside sell watermelons from the back of rusty pick-up trucks to supplement a paltry income from agriculture. Child beggars can be seen roaming the city streets, a sight which diplomats say is becoming increasingly common.
"The authorities know they have a time bomb on their hands," says one diplomat. "But Saudisation won't work without the necessary education for Saudis to fill the jobs now held by expatriates."
QUARTER OF BUDGET FOR EDUCATION

For 1997 the government allocated 41.7 billion riyals ($11.1 billion) -- almost a quarter of the budget -- for education, a move which analysts say highlights the country's determination to make the Saudi workforce more employable.
"But the emphasis in Saudi education is all wrong," one diplomat said. "There's too much religious education and too little practical work."
Another said: "In school they are increasingly learning this arch-conservative and even radical Islam, and they are learning it by rote and not learning how to think."
Diplomats say most Saudis frown at vocational training and consider a university degree far more prestigious.
"The result is that only about five percent of students go through the vocational training track," a diplomat who specialises in the issue said. "That's totally unsatisfactory."
Some progress has been made in the Saudisation drive, but citizens are only beginning to change their attitude towards work, diplomats said.

"Slowly, you are starting to see Saudis as chauffeurs, cashiers and messengers. That would have been unthinkable a few years ago," said one. "Slowly, they are learning that you don't automatically get a position as chairman of the board."
